what_you_do: For an unclear situation, you share 10 points of likelihood between several readings, then decide whether and how to find out what was meant.

method.name: Perspective-getting, and other readings of ambiguity
method.text: When information is missing, we often fill the gap with one reading, sometimes the most negative. Two things can help: considering several readings, and getting real information instead of guessing what someone else thinks.

research.text: A series of 25 experiments suggests that imagining how someone else sees things doesn't make people more accurate about what they think, and can make them more confident without being more accurate. Asking them helped.
research.who: 25 experiments · who took part and the settings to be confirmed from the full text

research.text: A review of 45 research reports suggests that repeated practice at reading ambiguous situations less negatively changes how people read new situations, but has only a small effect on anxiety and low mood.
research.who: 2,591 people · computer-based training, often over several sessions

research.text: A later review of 49 controlled trials suggests that even these small effects on anxiety and low mood disappear when unpublished results and extreme outliers are taken into account.
research.who: 49 randomised controlled trials · including people diagnosed with anxiety or depression

similar_note: The training research above repeated many scenarios over several sessions and always steered towards a positive reading. This exercise does neither: it's one visit, and you decide how likely each reading is. No research has tested this format.
about_this_exercise: This exercise draws on these methods, but this version hasn't been tested itself.
limits: Asking isn't always possible or wise.
Sharing out points shows how sure you feel, not what's true.
The research on reading ambiguity mostly measured effects in the lab.
